content.text: I'll read the tutorial notebook first, then look at the referenced vsim demo to understand how each engine handles syscalls.

<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andes-sim: a hands-on tutorial

`andes-sim` is one command that drives the Andes RISC-V simulators. This
notebook teaches it by running **real commands** against the binary built in
this repo. Each code cell is a plain shell command - the `!` prefix (or a `%%bash`
block) tells Jupyter to run it in the shell - so everything here is exactly what
you would type in a terminal.

## The mental model: one run = MODEL x ENGINE ( x TRIGGER )

To run something you pick up to three things:

| Axis | Question it answers | Choices |
|------|---------------------|---------|
| **model**   | which simulators run, and how they combine | `fast`, `cycle`, `hybrid` |
| **engine**  | which concrete simulator binary            | `qemu` (built in) or `vsim:<cpu>` (discovered) |
| **trigger** | (hybrid only) where the measured region starts and ends | `csr`, `pc`, `icount` |

The three models in one picture:

```
fast    QEMU only        fast (MHz speed), functional only, NO cycle count
cycle   one vsim only    cycle-accurate, but runs the WHOLE program in RTL (slow)
hybrid  QEMU  ->  vsim    QEMU fast-forwards; vsim measures only the region you pick
```

`hybrid` is the reason the tool exists: QEMU runs the boring parts quickly,
and the cycle-accurate vsim measures only the small region of interest (ROI).

> Note: `andes-sim` uses `--model` / `--engine` / `--trigger`. The older `./hsim`
> driver uses `--mode`; this tutorial is about `andes-sim`.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Setup

Prerequisites: the driver, the simulators, and the test fixtures are already
built (`build/andes-sim`, `verilator/build/sim_*`, `build/qemu/...`, the QEMU
plugin, and `tests/fixtures/*.elf`). If any are missing:

```sh
bash scripts/build_driver.sh      # the driver only
# or, everything:
source ./setup.sh                 # qemu + vsim + plugin + simpoint
make -C tests/fixtures -j         # the .elf fixtures
```

The single cell below is the only Python in this notebook: it finds the repo
root, switches to it, and puts `build/` on `PATH`, so every later cell can call
`!andes-sim` directly. (It walks up to the `build/andes-sim` binary, so there
is no hardcoded path - it works wherever the repo lives.)</cell id="cell-1">
<cell id="cell-2">import os
from pathlib import Path
root = next(str(d) for d in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
            if (d / "build" / "andes-sim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)</cell id="cell-2">

working dir: /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim

<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. Discover what is available

Start with `--help`. The release surface is deliberately small: just `run` and
`list`.</cell id="cell-3">
<cell id="cell-4">!andes-sim --help</cell id="cell-4">

usage: andes-sim <cmd> [args...]

Multi-engine driver for the Andes simulators (QEMU + vsim).

commands:
  run        run one simulation (--model fast|cycle|hybrid)
  list       list models|engines

(set ANDES_SIM_DEV=1 to show developer commands)

<cell id="cell-5"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Developer commands (`build`, `test`, `doctor`) are hidden by default and
appear only when `ANDES_SIM_DEV=1` is set. They are for working on the repo,
not for running simulations. You can set the variable inline for one command:</cell id="cell-5">
<cell id="cell-6">!ANDES_SIM_DEV=1 andes-sim --help</cell id="cell-6">

usage: andes-sim <cmd> [args...]

Multi-engine driver for the Andes simulators (QEMU + vsim).

commands:
  run        run one simulation (--model fast|cycle|hybrid)
  list       list models|engines

developer commands:
  build      build artifacts (qemu, vsim, plugin, simpoint, fixtures, driver)
  test       run the end-to-end suite
  doctor     check environment health

<cell id="cell-7"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`list models` shows the three compositions and what each is for.</cell id="cell-7">
<cell id="cell-8">!andes-sim list models</cell id="cell-8">

MODEL   ENGINES       NOTES
fast    qemu          functional
cycle   vsim:<cfg>    cycle-accurate
hybrid  qemu -> vsim  QEMU fast-forwards, vsim measures the ROI; pick --trigger csr|pc|icount

<cell id="cell-9"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`list engines` shows the concrete simulators. `qemu` is built in. The
`vsim:<cpu>` rows are discovered at runtime by scanning `verilator/build/` for
binaries that describe themselves, so building a new CPU config makes it appear
here with no code change.

- **KIND** is what the selector keys on: `functional` (QEMU) vs
  `cycle-accurate` (vsim). `cycle` and `hybrid` need a `cycle-accurate` engine.
- **VLEN** is the vector register width in bits (`-` means not reported).</cell id="cell-9">
<cell id="cell-10">!andes-sim list engines</cell id="cell-10">

ENGINE                 TYPE  KIND            VLEN
qemu                   qemu  functional      -
vsim:ax45mpv_mp2       vsim  cycle-accurate  512
vsim:ax45mpv_premium   vsim  cycle-accurate  512
vsim:ax46mpv_advanced  vsim  cycle-accurate  512
vsim:ax66_makatau      vsim  cycle-accurate  128
vsim:d23               vsim  cycle-accurate  -

<cell id="cell-11"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>> This repo has **five** cycle-accurate engines built. When more than one
> exists, `cycle` and `hybrid` cannot guess which to use, so you must name one
> with `--engine` (shown below). If only one were built, it would be picked
> automatically.</cell id="cell-11">
<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. Build a program, then run it on pure QEMU (`fast`)

`fast` runs an ELF on QEMU alone - a **transparent passthrough**: the program's
own input/output flows straight through and QEMU's exit code is propagated. Fast
and functional, but **no cycle count**.

For this section and the next we use one tiny program, the repo's `hello.c`,
compiled **once per engine** (QEMU here, verilator in section 3):

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { printf("hello\n"); return 0; }
```

Build it into `hello.adx` - just a RISC-V ELF (the extension is arbitrary; QEMU
loads it via `-bios`). A plain QEMU program does **not** need the test fixtures'
custom startup. `-mvh` (Andes virtual hosting) links the default startup plus the
`libgloss_vh` semihosting runtime, and the toolchain's default linker script
places it in `andes_ae350` DRAM. So the whole build is one line:</cell id="cell-12">
<cell id="cell-13">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN (also done by `source ./setup.sh`)
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

# -mvh = Andes virtual hosting: default startup + libgloss_vh semihosting.
"$GCC" -mvh hello.c -o hello.adx

echo "built hello.adx:"; file hello.adx</cell id="cell-13">

built hello.adx:


hello.adx: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), staticall

y linked, not stripped

<cell id="cell-14"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>On pure QEMU it prints `hello` and exits cleanly:</cell id="cell-14">
<cell id="cell-15">!andes-sim run --model fast hello.adx</cell id="cell-15">

hello

<cell id="cell-16"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 3. The same source on pure verilator (`cycle`) - a different build

`cycle` runs an ELF on a single verilator (vsim) engine **from reset**, in RTL -
cycle-accurate but slow, because it simulates the whole program at the gate
level.

**Verilator needs a different build than QEMU.** `-mvh`'s default startup assumes
a semihosting host, which vsim is not, so we cannot reuse `hello.adx`. For vsim we
build the *same* `hello.c` with the bare-metal runtime the test fixtures use -
`crt0.S` + `trap.S` + `handler.c` plus the `test.ld` linker script (load base
`0x00100000`), with `-nostartfiles -nodefaultlibs` (no `-mvh`):</cell id="cell-16">
<cell id="cell-17">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

# Bare-metal runtime for vsim (NO -mvh): explicit crt0/trap/handler + test.ld.
"$GCC" \
  -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 -static -nostartfiles -nodefaultlibs \
  -Itests/fixtures/runtime -Wall -T tests/fixtures/test.ld \
  tests/fixtures/runtime/crt0.S tests/fixtures/runtime/trap.S tests/fixtures/runtime/handler.c \
  hello.c \
  -Wl,--start-group -lc -lgloss_vh -lgcc -Wl,--end-group \
  -o hello_vsim.elf

echo "built hello_vsim.elf:"; file hello_vsim.elf</cell id="cell-17">

built hello_vsim.elf:


hello_vsim.elf: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), stat

ically linked, not stripped

<cell id="cell-18"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>This repo built several cycle-accurate engines, so `cycle` refuses to guess
and asks you to pick one with `--engine`:</cell id="cell-18">
<cell id="cell-19">!andes-sim run --model cycle hello_vsim.elf</cell id="cell-19">

andes-sim run --model cycle: model cycle: multiple cycle-accurate engines; select one with --engine (have: vsim:ax45mpv_mp2, vsim:ax45mpv_premium, vsim:ax46mpv_advanced, vsim:ax66_makatau, vsim:d23)

<cell id="cell-20"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Now name an engine. We cap it with `timeout` - watch what is, and is not, printed:</cell id="cell-20">
<cell id="cell-21">!timeout 25 andes-sim run --model cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello_vsim.elf </dev/null</cell id="cell-21">

Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown



[[32minfo[m] loading segment: addr=0x100000, memsz=37112, filesz=36136
[[32minfo[m] hart 0 reset vector: 0x100000

<cell id="cell-22"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>**It loads and boots, but never prints `hello`.** vsim runs the bare-metal
`crt0` fine (no semihosting there), but the first `printf` in `main` makes a
**semihosting** system call, and vsim does **not** implement semihosting - the
call traps, and the fixture's `handler.c` cannot even report it (its error
message is itself a semihosting write). So nothing escapes and the program never
exits; only the `timeout` ends it. See `docs/vsim_semihosting_investigation.md`.

Compare with section 2: on pure QEMU `hello.adx` printed `hello` and exited 0,
because QEMU services semihosting. This is exactly why **hybrid** exists - let
QEMU handle the semihosting-heavy parts (boot, I/O, teardown) and let verilator
measure only a compute region that issues no system calls.</cell id="cell-22">
<cell id="cell-23"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 4. Model `hybrid` - the headline

`hybrid` runs two legs in one command:

```
QEMU1  -- drained state + shared memory -->  vsim
(fast-forward to the ROI)                    (measure the ROI, then drain)
```

The result is **window_cycles**: the vsim cycle count for the region, measured
as `vsim mcycle - qemu mcycle`. The result lines go to **stdout** (an
`[hsim mmap]` line, the `[... window_cycles] N` line, and a `PASS:` line); the
`[andes-sim] model=... engine=... trigger=...` banner goes to **stderr**. With
`!` you see both in the cell.

The **trigger** decides where the measured region begins and ends:

| Trigger | Profiles          | How the region is delimited |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| `csr`   | a kernel you mark | two `csrwi 0x7C0, 0/1` markers compiled into the source |
| `pc`    | a kernel          | two explicit PCs you pass (`--pc-start`, `--pc-end`); a symbol or `0x` address |
| `icount`| a sampled window  | instruction counts: fast-forward N, then measure M (no markers) |

> The absolute `mcycle=...` numbers are a free-running counter and differ on
> every run. The bracketed `window_cycles` value is the figure you care about,
> and it is deterministic for a given ELF + engine + trigger.</cell id="cell-23">
<cell id="cell-24"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>These hybrid examples use the RVV GEMM fixtures, not the `hello` builds:
hybrid measures a compute *region of interest*, and `hello` only does I/O (which
must stay on QEMU) with no compute to measure.

### 4a. trigger `csr` - measure a marked kernel

`rt_c_v_matmul.elf` wraps its kernel in the two `csrwi 0x7C0, 0/1` markers, so
the trigger needs no parameters. This is the canonical example.</cell id="cell-24">
<cell id="cell-25">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger csr --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf</cell id="cell-25">

[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=csr fixture=rt_c_v_matmul
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)


[csr window_cycles] 22808  (vsim mcycle=695138073055008 - qemu mcycle=695138073032200)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger csr (rt_c_v_matmul)

<cell id="cell-26"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4b. trigger `pc` - measure between two PCs

When the binary has no markers, pass the boundary PCs yourself. `--pc-start`
accepts a **symbol name** (andes-sim resolves it from the ELF) or a `0x` address;
`--pc-end` is the same. Both are required.

`rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf` is the markerless twin of the kernel above. We start at
the `vmatmul_kernel` symbol and end at the return point after its call in `main`
(`0x1002c4`). To find that address yourself, disassemble and read the
instruction right after `jal ... <vmatmul_kernel>`:

```sh
$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf | grep -A1 'jal.*vmatmul_kernel'
```</cell id="cell-26">
<cell id="cell-27">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --pc-start vmatmul_kernel --pc-end 0x1002c4 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf</cell id="cell-27">

[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=pc fixture=rt_c_v_matmul_free
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)


[pc window_cycles] 22769  (vsim mcycle=695196736797057 - qemu mcycle=695196736774288)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger pc (rt_c_v_matmul_free)

<cell id="cell-28"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`pc` and `csr` should report nearly the same cycle count here - both wrap
the same single `vmatmul_kernel` call. The small difference is where each
boundary lands relative to the marker instructions.</cell id="cell-28">
<cell id="cell-29"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4c. trigger `icount` - sample a window by instruction count

For workloads you cannot edit and do not want to mark. QEMU fast-forwards
`--qemu-icount` instructions, then vsim measures `--vsim-icount` instructions and
drains. No markers needed. Defaults are `10000` / `5000`.</cell id="cell-29">
<cell id="cell-30">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger icount --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --qemu-icount 2000 --vsim-icount 1000 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf</cell id="cell-30">

[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=icount fixture=rt_c_v_matmul_free
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)


[icount window_cycles] 13182  (vsim mcycle=695261073781814 - qemu mcycle=695261073768632)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger icount (rt_c_v_matmul_free)

<cell id="cell-31"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 5. Picking an engine with `--engine`

`--engine <id>` selects which simulator to use. For `fast` it must be `qemu`
(the only functional engine). For `cycle` and `hybrid` it names one of the
`vsim:<cpu>` rows from `list engines`. Different CPU configs have different
microarchitectures and VLEN, so the same workload reports different cycles.

Try it yourself - rerun the csr example (section 4a) on a different core and
compare the number:

```sh
andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger csr --engine vsim:ax45mpv_mp2 \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf
```

A heavier core simulates more slowly. If a leg exceeds the built-in 90 s per-leg
timeout, andes-sim stops it with `plan step 1: timed out after 90000 ms`; in that
case measure a smaller window (e.g. `--trigger icount` with small counts) or pick
a lighter core.</cell id="cell-31">
<cell id="cell-32"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 6. Forwarding native engine flags with `--`

Everything after a lone `--` is passed to the engine **verbatim**; andes-sim does
not interpret it. This lets you use an engine's own command line - for example a
gdbstub on the functional engine (QEMU opens a gdb server on `:1234` and waits):

```sh

# andes-sim: a hands-on tutorial

`andes-sim` is one command that drives the Andes RISC-V simulators. This
notebook teaches it by running **real commands** against the binary built in
this repo. Each code cell is a plain shell command - the `!` prefix (or a `%%bash`
block) tells Jupyter to run it in the shell - so everything here is exactly what
you would type in a terminal.

## The mental model: one run = MODEL x ENGINE ( x TRIGGER )

To run something you pick up to three things:

| Axis | Question it answers | Choices |
|------|---------------------|---------|
| **model**   | which simulators run, and how they combine | `fast`, `cycle`, `hybrid` |
| **engine**  | which concrete simulator binary            | `qemu` (built in) or `vsim:<cpu>` (discovered) |
| **trigger** | (hybrid only) where the measured region starts and ends | `csr`, `pc`, `icount` |

The three models in one picture:

```
fast    QEMU only        fast (MHz speed), functional only, NO cycle count
cycle   one vsim only    cycle-accurate, but runs the WHOLE program in RTL (slow)
hybrid  QEMU  ->  vsim    QEMU fast-forwards; vsim measures only the region you pick
```

`hybrid` is the reason the tool exists: QEMU runs the boring parts quickly,
and the cycle-accurate vsim measures only the small region of interest (ROI).

> Note: `andes-sim` uses `--model` / `--engine` / `--trigger`. The older `./hsim`
> driver uses `--mode`; this tutorial is about `andes-sim`.

## Setup

Prerequisites: the driver, the simulators, and the test fixtures are already
built (`build/andes-sim`, `verilator/build/sim_*`, `build/qemu/...`, the QEMU
plugin, and `tests/fixtures/*.elf`). If any are missing:

```sh
bash scripts/build_driver.sh      # the driver only
# or, everything:
source ./setup.sh                 # qemu + vsim + plugin + simpoint
make -C tests/fixtures -j         # the .elf fixtures
```

The single cell below is the only Python in this notebook: it finds the repo
root, switches to it, and puts `build/` on `PATH`, so every later cell can call
`!andes-sim` directly. (It walks up to the `build/andes-sim` binary, so there
is no hardcoded path - it works wherever the repo lives.)

import os
from pathlib import Path
root = next(str(d) for d in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
            if (d / "build" / "andes-sim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)

`list engines` shows the concrete simulators. `qemu` is built in. The

here with no code change.

- **KIND** is what the selector keys on: `functional` (QEMU) vs
  `cycle-accurate` (vsim). `cycle` and `hybrid` need a `cycle-accurate` engine.
- **VLEN** is the vector register width in bits (`-` means not reported).
!andes-sim list engines

outputs.text:

qemu                   qemu  functional      -
vsim:ax45mpv_mp2       vsim  cycle-accurate  512
vsim:ax45mpv_premium   vsim  cycle-accurate  512

> This repo has **five** cycle-accurate engines built. When more than one
> exists, `cycle` and `hybrid` cannot guess which to use, so you must name one
> with `--engine` (shown below). If only one were built, it would be picked

## 2. Build a program, then run it on pure QEMU (`fast`)

`fast` runs an ELF on QEMU alone - a **transparent passthrough**: the program's
own input/output flows straight through and QEMU's exit code is propagated. Fast
and functional, but **no cycle count**.

For this section and the next we use one tiny program, the repo's `hello.c`,
compiled **once per engine** (QEMU here, verilator in section 3):

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { printf("hello\n"); return 0; }
```

Build it into `hello.adx` - just a RISC-V ELF (the extension is arbitrary; QEMU
loads it via `-bios`). A plain QEMU program does **not** need the test fixtures'
custom startup. `-mvh` (Andes virtual hosting) links the default startup plus the
`libgloss_vh` semihosting runtime, and the toolchain's default linker script
places it in `andes_ae350` DRAM. So the whole build is one line:

%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN (also done by `source ./setup.sh`)
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

# -mvh = Andes virtual hosting: default startup + libgloss_vh semihosting.
"$GCC" -mvh hello.c -o hello.adx

echo "built hello.adx:"; file hello.adx

outputs.text: built hello.adx:
hello.adx: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), staticall
y linked, not stripped

cells.source: On pure QEMU it prints `hello` and exits cleanly:
!andes-sim run --model fast hello.adx

outputs.text: hello

cells.source:
## 3. The same source on pure verilator (`cycle`) - a different build

`cycle` runs an ELF on a single verilator (vsim) engine **from reset**, in RTL -
cycle-accurate but slow, because it simulates the whole program at the gate
level.

**Verilator needs a different build than QEMU.** `-mvh`'s default startup assumes
a semihosting host, which vsim is not, so we cannot reuse `hello.adx`. For vsim we
build the *same* `hello.c` with the bare-metal runtime the test fixtures use -
`crt0.S` + `trap.S` + `handler.c` plus the `test.ld` linker script (load base
`0x00100000`), with `-nostartfiles -nodefaultlibs` (no `-mvh`):

%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

# Bare-metal runtime for vsim (NO -mvh): explicit crt0/trap/handler + test.ld.
"$GCC" \
  -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 -static -nostartfiles -nodefaultlibs \
  -Itests/fixtures/runtime -Wall -T tests/fixtures/test.ld \
  tests/fixtures/runtime/crt0.S tests/fixtures/runtime/trap.S tests/fixtures/runtime/handler.c \
  hello.c \
  -Wl,--start-group -lc -lgloss_vh -lgcc -Wl,--end-group \
  -o hello_vsim.elf

echo "built hello_vsim.elf:"; file hello_vsim.elf

outputs.text: built hello_vsim.elf:
hello_vsim.elf: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), stat
ically linked, not stripped

cells.source:
This repo built several cycle-accurate engines, so `cycle` refuses to guess
and asks you to pick one with `--engine`:
!andes-sim run --model cycle hello_vsim.elf

outputs.text: andes-sim run --model cycle: model cycle: multiple cycle-accurate engines; select one with --engine (have: vsim:ax45mpv_mp2, vsim:ax45mpv_premium, vsim:ax46mpv_advanced, vsim:ax66_makatau, vsim:d23)

cells.source: Now name an engine. We cap it with `timeout` - watch what is, and is not, printed:
!timeout 25 andes-sim run --model cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello_vsim.elf </dev/null

outputs.text:
Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown

[[32minfo[m] loading segment: addr=0x100000, memsz=37112, filesz=36136
[[32minfo[m] hart 0 reset vector: 0x100000

cells.source:
**It loads and boots, but never prints `hello`.** vsim runs the bare-metal
`crt0` fine (no semihosting there), but the first `printf` in `main` makes a
**semihosting** system call, and vsim does **not** implement semihosting - the
call traps, and the fixture's `handler.c` cannot even report it (its error
message is itself a semihosting write). So nothing escapes and the program never
exits; only the `timeout` ends it. See `docs/vsim_semihosting_investigation.md`.

Compare with section 2: on pure QEMU `hello.adx` printed `hello` and exited 0,
because QEMU services semihosting. This is exactly why **hybrid** exists - let
QEMU handle the semihosting-heavy parts (boot, I/O, teardown) and let verilator
measure only a compute region that issues no system calls.

## 4. Model `hybrid` - the headline

`hybrid` runs two legs in one command:

```
QEMU1  -- drained state + shared memory -->  vsim
(fast-forward to the ROI)                    (measure the ROI, then drain)
```

The result is **window_cycles**: the vsim cycle count for the region, measured
as `vsim mcycle - qemu mcycle`. The result lines go to **stdout** (an
`[hsim mmap]` line, the `[... window_cycles] N` line, and a `PASS:` line); the
`[andes-sim] model=... engine=... trigger=...` banner goes to **stderr**. With
`!` you see both in the cell.

The **trigger** decides where the measured region begins and ends:

| Trigger | Profiles          | How the region is delimited |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| `csr`   | a kernel you mark | two `csrwi 0x7C0, 0/1` markers compiled into the source |
| `pc`    | a kernel          | two explicit PCs you pass (`--pc-start`, `--pc-end`); a symbol or `0x` address |
| `icount`| a sampled window  | instruction counts: fast-forward N, then measure M (no markers) |

> The absolute `mcycle=...` numbers are a free-running counter and differ on
> every run. The bracketed `window_cycles` value is the figure you care about,
> and it is deterministic for a given ELF + engine + trigger.

These hybrid examples use the RVV GEMM fixtures, not the `hello` builds:
hybrid measures a compute *region of interest*, and `hello` only does I/O (which
must stay on QEMU) with no compute to measure.

### 4a. trigger `csr` - measure a marked kernel

`rt_c_v_matmul.elf` wraps its kernel in the two `csrwi 0x7C0, 0/1` markers, so
the trigger needs no parameters. This is the canonical example.
!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger csr --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf

outputs.text:
[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=csr fixture=rt_c_v_matmul
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)

[csr window_cycles] 22808  (vsim mcycle=695138073055008 - qemu mcycle=695138073032200)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger csr (rt_c_v_matmul)

cells.source:
### 4b. trigger `pc` - measure between two PCs

When the binary has no markers, pass the boundary PCs yourself. `--pc-start`
accepts a **symbol name** (andes-sim resolves it from the ELF) or a `0x` address;
`--pc-end` is the same. Both are required.

`rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf` is the markerless twin of the kernel above. We start at
the `vmatmul_kernel` symbol and end at the return point after its call in `main`
(`0x1002c4`). To find that address yourself, disassemble and read the
instruction right after `jal ... <vmatmul_kernel>`:

```sh
$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf | grep -A1 'jal.*vmatmul_kernel'
```
!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --pc-start vmatmul_kernel --pc-end 0x1002c4 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf

outputs.text:
[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=pc fixture=rt_c_v_matmul_free
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)

[pc window_cycles] 22769  (vsim mcycle=695196736797057 - qemu mcycle=695196736774288)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger pc (rt_c_v_matmul_free)

cells.source:
`pc` and `csr` should report nearly the same cycle count here - both wrap
the same single `vmatmul_kernel` call. The small difference is where each
boundary lands relative to the marker instructions.

### 4c. trigger `icount` - sample a window by instruction count

For workloads you cannot edit and do not want to mark. QEMU fast-forwards
`--qemu-icount` instructions, then vsim measures `--vsim-icount` instructions and
drains. No markers needed. Defaults are `10000` / `5000`.
!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger icount --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --qemu-icount 2000 --vsim-icount 1000 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf

outputs.text:
[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium trigger=icount fixture=rt_c_v_matmul_free
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)

[icount window_cycles] 13182  (vsim mcycle=695261073781814 - qemu mcycle=695261073768632)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger icount (rt_c_v_matmul_free)

cells.source:
## 5. Picking an engine with `--engine`

`--engine <id>` selects which simulator to use. For `fast` it must be `qemu`
(the only functional engine). For `cycle` and `hybrid` it names one of the
`vsim:<cpu>` rows from `list engines`. Different CPU configs have different
microarchitectures and VLEN, so the same workload reports different cycles.

Try it yourself - rerun the csr example (section 4a) on a different core and
compare the number:

```sh
andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger csr --engine vsim:ax45mpv_mp2 \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf
```

A heavier core simulates more slowly. If a leg exceeds the built-in 90 s per-leg
timeout, andes-sim stops it with `plan step 1: timed out after 90000 ms`; in that
case measure a smaller window (e.g. `--trigger icount` with small counts) or pick
a lighter core.

## 6. Forwarding native engine flags with `--`

Everything after a lone `--` is passed to the engine **verbatim**; andes-sim does
not interpret it. This lets you use an engine's own command line - for example a
gdbstub on the functional engine (QEMU opens a gdb server on `:1234` and waits):

```sh
andes-sim run --model fast tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf -- -gdb tcp::1234 -S
```

The `--` boundary is what lets `fast` and `cycle` expose the full native CLI of
their engine, so you can attach a debugger, a monitor, or a console exactly as if
you had launched the simulator directly. (Not run here - it blocks waiting for a
debugger.)

## 7. Developer commands (optional)

Set `ANDES_SIM_DEV=1` to reveal `build`, `test`, and `doctor` (section 1). They
build the artifacts, run the end-to-end suite, and check environment health -
useful when working on the repo, not when just running simulations. For most
build/test work the documented entry points are `bash scripts/build_driver.sh`,
`source ./setup.sh`, and `bash scripts/run_e2e.sh` (use `JOBS=8`).

## 8. Cheat sheet and where to go next

```sh
andes-sim list models                        # the 3 compositions
andes-sim list engines                        # the concrete simulators
andes-sim run --model fast  ELF               # QEMU only, functional
andes-sim run --model cycle --engine vsim:<cpu> ELF        # one vsim, from reset
andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger csr    --engine vsim:<cpu> ELF
andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc     --engine vsim:<cpu> --pc-start S --pc-end E ELF
andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger icount --engine vsim:<cpu> --qemu-icount N --vsim-icount M ELF
```

# vsim Semihosting Investigation

> SUPERSEDED 2026-06-09: the vsim -> QEMU2 handback was removed repo-wide; the simulator is now 2-phase (QEMU1 drain -> vsim drain). See remove_qemu2.md. The QEMU2/handback content below is historical.

Scope: can we port QEMU's RISC-V semihosting into the Verilator-based vsim so
that binaries linked with `-mvh` (Andes virtual hosting, `libgloss_vh`) can
perform I/O system calls on both QEMU and vsim?

This document answers step 1 only: how the current vsim handles those system
calls today.

## Bottom Line

vsim does NOT implement semihosting. Every guest syscall trap is fatal.
The fixtures work around this with the Phase-2 rule: no libc I/O between
`enter_vsim()` and `exit_vsim()`.

## Current vsim Trap Flow

1. `libgloss_vh` in the Andes toolchain compiles `printf` / `_write` /
   `_exit` / `_sbrk` down to the RISC-V semihosting magic triple:

   ```
   slli x0, x0, 0x1f    # at mepc - 4
   ebreak               # at mepc
   srai x0, x0, 0x7     # at mepc + 4
   ```

2. vsim's hart takes a breakpoint exception at `ebreak` (mcause = 3) and
   jumps to `mtvec`.

3. `mtvec` points to the fixture's own trap stub:
   `tests/fixtures/runtime/trap.S:19-120` saves all GPRs/CSRs and
   calls `handle_trap()`.

4. `tests/fixtures/runtime/handler.c:23-52` reads `mcause`,
   `mdcause`, `mepc`, `mtval` via inline CSR reads, prints
   `[ERROR] Trap occurred!` to stderr through libgloss, then calls
   `_exit(mcause)`.

Critical: `handler.c` never inspects the bytes around `mepc` to recognize
the magic triple. The comment at `handler.c:4-6` admits this:

> libgloss_vh routes syscalls through the RISC-V semihosting magic triple,
> not through `ecall`, so there is no syscall-dispatch table here. Any trap
> is treated as a fatal error.

That is why CLAUDE.md and `runtime/rt_c_helpers.h:2-9` carry the Phase-2
rule: between `enter_vsim()` and `exit_vsim()` the fixture must not call
any libc I/O function. Phase 1 and Phase 3 print fine because both QEMUs
are launched with `-semihosting-config enable=on,target=native`.

## Why the Phase-2 Rule Exists in Code

- `tests/fixtures/Makefile:22-24` -- comment explaining libgloss_vh
  and that "vsim does not implement semihosting."
- `tests/fixtures/runtime/rt_c_helpers.h:2-9` -- documents that
  inside the span the magic triple would route to mtvec and loop.
- `verilator/src/hybrid/qemu_handback.hpp` -- launches QEMU2 with
  `-semihosting-config` so Phase 3 I/O still works.
- `verilator/src/main.cpp:114` -- mentions semihosting only as part of
  QEMU2 launch docs.

Grep across `verilator/` for `semihosting`, `sys_write`, `SYS_WRITE`,
`SYS_READ`, `_sbrk` returns no implementation, only those references.

## How QEMU Does the Same Thing (Reference)

- Detect: `QEMU/target/riscv/insn_trans/trans_privileged.c.inc:28-70`
  decodes `ebreak`, reads `[mepc-4, mepc+4]`, matches the triple, then
  raises `RISCV_EXCP_SEMIHOST` instead of `RISCV_EXCP_BREAKPOINT`.
- Target glue (RV-specific arg/ret regs):
  `QEMU/target/riscv/common-semi-target.h:14-26` -- args in `a0/a1`,
  return value placed in `a0`.
- Dispatcher (around 20 syscalls, ARM Semihosting v2.0):
  `QEMU/semihosting/arm-compat-semi.c` and
  `QEMU/semihosting/syscalls.c`. Implements `SYS_OPEN`, `SYS_CLOSE`,
  `SYS_READ`, `SYS_WRITE`, `SYS_SEEK`, `SYS_FLEN`, `SYS_STAT`, `SYS_ISTTY`,
  `SYS_HEAPINFO`, `SYS_EXIT`, `SYS_EXIT_EXTENDED`, and more.

RISC-V reuses the ARM Semihosting v2.0 spec verbatim via the magic triple;
it is not a RISC-V-specific variant.

## libgloss_vh / -mvh Details

- `-mvh` is an Andes toolchain flag that selects virtual hosting mode,
  routing I/O through the semihosting magic triple instead of through
  ecall / proxy-kernel.
- `tests/fixtures/Makefile:39-44` link order:

  ```
  RT_C_LIBS := -Wl,--start-group -lc -lgloss_vh -lgcc -Wl,--end-group
  ```

- `-lgloss_vh` provides `_write`, `_exit`, `_sbrk`, `_read`, ... built
  on the magic triple. Source is not in this repo; it ships in the Andes
  toolchain.

## vsim Host-Side Hooks Available Today

There is no DPI-C bridge, SystemC export, or printf-debug channel from
guest to host. The only existing guest-to-host paths are:

- The DMI bus (Debug Module) that `ResumeDriver` and `StateDrain` already
  use to read and write GPRs / FPRs / CSRs / V-state.
- The shared `/dev/shm` mmap region (Tier-2 fixtures) -- the host process
  can read it concurrently while the hart runs.
- `mtvec` running guest code that the fixture itself controls.

vsim's main entry is `sc_main()` in `verilator/src/main.cpp`. It uses
`spdlog` and `fmt` for host-side logging; the guest cannot reach those.

## Two Natural Integration Points for a Port

1. Guest-side, in-trap: extend `handle_trap()` in
   `tests/fixtures/runtime/handler.c` to detect the magic triple
   (read bytes at `mepc-4` and `mepc+4`), emulate the syscall, write the
   result into `a0` in the trap frame, advance `mepc` by 4, and return.
   I/O reaches the host via the existing `/dev/shm` mmap (a tail-reader
   on the host turns the mmap region into stdout).
   - Pros: zero vsim core changes; isolated to the fixture runtime.
   - Cons: needs a mmap-based stdio protocol; harder for `SYS_OPEN` /
     `SYS_READ` against arbitrary host files; not the same path as QEMU.

2. Host-side, over DMI: the `handoff_controller` watches for the
   semihosting exception via DMI (same way it already watches CSR
   triggers), pauses the hart, reads `a0..a7` via Abstract Commands,
   executes the syscall on the host, writes `a0` back, advances `mepc`
   by 4, and resumes the hart.
   - Pros: architecturally equivalent to QEMU; full POSIX surface
     available; no guest-side runtime changes.
   - Cons: needs a new trigger path in `handoff_controller` and a new
     syscall dispatcher module under `verilator/src/hybrid/`.

Next step (not in this doc): pick one of the two integration points and
sketch it end-to-end -- syscall list, register-read order, `mepc` fixup,
file-descriptor table.

content.text:
## Answer

Make the **AE350 device ABI the single contract**: stdio through the 16550 UART (already modeled identically in both engines), exit and file syscalls through vsim's SimControl/HTIF block, and **add that one missing SimControl device to the QEMU fork**. Then one runtime library + one linker script gives you one `hello.elf` that runs unchanged on `fast`, `cycle`, and `hybrid`. Do not port semihosting into vsim - reasoning below.

## What I verified

| Guest-to-host channel | QEMU ae350 | vsim (repo submodule) |
|---|---|---|
| Semihosting magic triple (`-mvh`) | yes | **no** - fatal trap (`docs/vsim_semihosting_investigation.md`) |
| 16550 UART @ `0xf0200000`/`0xf0300000` | yes (`QEMU/hw/riscv/andes_ae350.c:104`) | yes (`verilator/src/platform/uart.hpp`, prints THR to host stdout) |
| SimControl exit @ `0xe0080000` | **no** - unmapped (memmap jumps from DRAM to MAC@`0xe0100000`) | yes (`verilator/src/platform/sim_control.hpp:160`, exit codes 0x01234568/9 or raw code) |
| HTIF file syscalls @ `0xe0080010` | **no** | yes - full 17-syscall host dispatcher (open/read/write/lseek/stat/...) in `sim_control.hpp:73-90` |

So the internal vsim demo (`/local/nick/vsim-demo-new`) already solved "syscalls on vsim" with `bsp_custom/libgloss.c`: newlib stubs route fd 0-2 to the UART, file ops to HTIF `frontend_syscall`, and `_exit` to the magic write. Its only gap is that QEMU does not implement SimControl, so today you need two builds. The repo's `verilator/` submodule ships the exact same UART + SimControl + HTIF models, so the gap is only on the QEMU side - and you own that fork.

## Why this design (and not the others)

The hard constraint comes from hybrid: **the same process migrates from QEMU to vsim mid-run**, and only RAM + architectural state move across. So:

- **Boot-time engine detection is impossible.** Any "which engine am I on" flag set at startup goes stale after the handoff. The binary must be engine-blind, which means every syscall channel it uses must exist on *both* engines. That kills the "link three runtimes, pick at boot" idea and the per-call detection idea (detection itself needs a probe device on both sides, so you end up building the unified device anyway, plus two code paths to maintain).
- **Port semihosting into vsim** (option 2 in the investigation doc) is the other comprehensive route: stock `-mvh` binaries would run everywhere. I recommend against it as the primary path because (a) each syscall must halt the hart over DMI, service on host, fix `mepc`, resume - heavy machinery inside the cycle-accurate engine, and the halt/resume perturbs exactly the window you are trying to measure; (b) MMIO-based I/O is what real silicon does, so UART cycles inside a measured region are *honest* cycles, while semihosting cycles are fiction; (c) it duplicates a 17-syscall dispatcher vsim already has.
- **Status quo (two builds)** fails your "compile once" requirement outright.

With the device-ABI design, hybrid degrades gracefully instead of hanging: a stray `printf` inside the ROI goes out the modeled UART (real cycles, still discouraged for clean measurement), and `exit()` inside vsim terminates the sim with a code instead of today's infinite loop. The Phase-2 "no syscalls" rule becomes a measurement-hygiene guideline, not a correctness cliff.

## The pieces to build

1. **`runtime/vplat/` (one runtime, new, in this repo)** - adapt `bsp_custom/libgloss.c` + `htif.h` from the demo:
   - `_write(fd<=2)` -> UART1 THR poll (works on both engines today, zero simulator changes)
   - `_exit` -> store exit code to `0xe0080000`, then spin
   - file ops -> HTIF magicmem + `tohost` write at `0xe0080010` (keep the demo's dcache flush before each call - SimControl reads magicmem behind the cache)
   - `_sbrk` -> `_end` heap (pure RAM, migrates through the shared mmap)
   - reuse `tests/fixtures/runtime/crt0.S` + `test.ld` (base `0x100000` is valid RAM on both: vsim RAM `0x0-0x7FFFFFFF`, QEMU DRAM `0x0-0x80000000`)
2. **QEMU fork: `andes_sim_control` device at `0xe0080000`** (~200 lines, the only simulator change): exit command -> shutdown with exit code; HTIF cmd -> read 8x u64 magicmem from guest DRAM, dispatch the same syscall numbers to the host, write `a0` back. Mirror `sim_control.hpp` semantics exactly so the device behaves identically on both sides.
3. **andes-sim driver**: propagate the SimControl exit code in `fast` (serial console output already flows through `-nographic`); `cycle` already returns `sim_control.exits`.
4. **Tutorial**: sections 2-3 collapse to one build cell; the same ELF runs in all three model cells - which is exactly the story the notebook wants to tell.

Build line becomes one command for all engines:

```sh
$GCC hello.c -o hello.elf -T runtime/vplat/vplat.ld runtime/vplat/crt0.S runtime/vplat/libgloss_vplat.c ...
```

## Open items

- Verify the Andes CCTL CSRs (`mcctlcommand`) used by the pre-HTIF cache flush are accepted by QEMU (likely yes in the Andes fork; harmless no-op is fine).
- Decide whether `-mvh` compatibility still matters for `fast`-only users; it keeps working, it just is not the portable build.
- Multi-hart `hello` (the demo's spinlock version) is out of scope for the first cut.

If you want, the next step is a ROADMAP-style breakdown (runtime lib -> QEMU device -> driver exit code -> tutorial rewrite) as a repo .md for your review.
